# The Quiet Art of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the spaces we don't pay attention to. Not the dramatic moments—those are easy enough to notice. The job offer. The breakup. The accident. The achievement. Those moments announce themselves; they demand our attention and rearrange our lives accordingly. But I'm interested in the other moments. The ones that slip past almost unnoticed, only to reveal their significance years later, if at all.

This came to me recently while I was sitting in my car during my lunch break, which is something I do most days. I park near a small park with big old trees and watch people pass by. It's not a scenic overlook or a philosophical destination. It's just a spot off a secondary road where I can be relatively alone without actually being alone. And while I sit there, I notice things. A woman always walks by at about 12:15 with her dog—not the same day every week, but frequently enough that I've started to expect her. The dog is elderly, moves slowly, and she never hurries it. Sometimes I wonder where she's going, whether she's happy, what her name is. I'll never know, and that's somehow perfect.

I think we're trained to overlook most of what happens around us. Modern life seems designed to pull our attention toward the significant, the urgent, the quantifiable. How many steps did you take today? How many likes did your post receive? What's your productivity score? What did you accomplish? The pressure to measure and optimize everything has become so normalized that we've forgotten how to be still and simply present. We've forgotten—or perhaps we've been encouraged to forget—that noticing itself is a kind of accomplishment. That seeing someone fully, or really tasting your food, or listening to the actual sound of rain, or noticing how the light changes throughout the day, is itself valuable.

There's a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the pathos of things. It's the bittersweet awareness of the transience of all things, and the kind of poignancy that emerges from that awareness. The way cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they're fleeting. The way a photograph becomes precious because it captures something that no longer exists in that form. The way you suddenly become aware that a friend you've known your whole life will someday no longer be in your life, and that awareness somehow deepens your feeling for them in the present moment. This seems like the opposite of modern culture, which tries to preserve, extend, quantify, and make permanent everything. Yet it might be the most honest way of being in the world.

I think about my grandmother, who passed away two years ago. She had this habit of sitting in her kitchen in the morning with a cup of tea, looking out the window. She wasn't doing anything, not meditating in any formal sense. She was just sitting there. Sometimes she'd comment on what she saw: "The cardinal's back." "The hydrangeas are starting to turn." "It looks like rain." For years I thought of this as a waste of her time—shouldn't she be reading, or doing a puzzle, or at least engaged in something purposeful? But now I understand that she was engaged in something purposeful. She was actually living her life instead of rushing through it. She was present. She was noticing.

After she died, I found a stack of her old photographs. Not the formal posed pictures, but the casual ones. Photos of doorways, of gardens, of the way light fell across a wall. Photos of her children as teenagers, candid and often blurry. Photos of trees. So many photographs of trees. At the time they were taken, these probably seemed unremarkable enough to capture but not important enough to obsess over. But looking at them now, I realize she was collecting moments. She was noticing what she wanted to remember. And more importantly, the very act of noticing—of deciding that something was worth photographing—meant that she was really seeing it.

This is starting to feel like the real purpose of consciousness, actually. Not achievement or acquisition or even happiness in the conventional sense, but this capacity to notice, to witness, to be aware of the texture of existence. We're the universe's way of looking at itself. That's what I mean when I say noticing is a form of accomplishment. It's not about productivity or external validation. It's about the fact that you were present for your own life.

There's something else I want to talk about, which is the way that noticing creates a kind of intimacy with the world. When you pay attention to something—really pay attention—a shift happens. It's subtle, but it's real. The person you keep seeing on the bus becomes less like a background element in your life and more like a person with an interior. The coffee shop where you work three days a week starts to feel like a place with character and history. The street you drive down every day reveals details you'd never seen before: a particular garden, a blue door, the way the houses are numbered. And these aren't things you needed to know. They won't help you achieve your goals or increase your net worth. But they make your life richer. They make you feel less alone. They make you part of something.

I think loneliness in modern society might have something to do with this. We're surrounded by people but don't really see them. We're in places but don't really inhabit them. We're distracted—perpetually, systematically distracted—by devices and obligations and the constant pressure to be productive, to improve, to move on to the next thing. And in the absence of real noticing, real attention, real presence, we feel isolated even when we're not alone.

There's a meditation practice where you focus on one thing—your breath, a candle flame, the sensation of your feet on the ground—and whenever your mind wanders (and it will wander constantly), you gently bring it back. The practice isn't really about achieving some permanent state of focus. It's about noticing when you've wandered and practicing the act of returning. Over time, what develops isn't a permanently tranquil mind, but a kind of friendly awareness of your own mind. You get to know it. You notice its patterns. And there's something deeply soothing about that—about being known to yourself.

I think the same thing happens when you practice noticing the external world. You develop a kind of gentle awareness of what's actually happening around you. You become more present. And yes, there's sadness in this awareness—sadness at the transience of things, sadness at all the moments you missed before you learned to notice them. But there's also profound gratitude. And gratitude, I think, might be the closest thing we have to genuine happiness.

I've been reading a lot of poetry lately, partly because poetry is the art form of noticing. Poets spend their time paying intense attention to small things: the way light looks on water, the feeling of your hand being held, the sound of a particular word. And somehow by noticing these things with such care, they manage to capture something essential about what it means to be alive. A good poem makes you feel less alone because it makes you realize that the small thing you noticed and thought was unique to your experience is actually a universal human thing. We all notice the way certain people have certain laughs. We all forget why we walked into a room. We all have looked at someone we love and felt a sudden crushing awareness that they will not always be here.

I want to write about my childhood for a moment because I realize that children are natural noticers. When you're young, everything is new, so you pay attention to everything. The way your grandmother smells. The taste of a particular food. The exact quality of light in a specific room. The sound of a particular person's voice. You notice without trying. But then you grow up and you're told to focus on what matters, and what matters is usually defined as what's measurable, what's productive, what contributes to your standing in the world. And so you train yourself to ignore most of what's actually happening. You lose that beginner's mind. You see what you expect to see rather than what's actually there.

One of my earliest memories is of lying in the grass behind my house when I was maybe five or six years old. I was just lying there, looking at the sky, noticing the shapes of clouds, feeling the grass prickle against the back of my neck. A bug crawled across my arm and I watched it, fascinated. A bird flew overhead and I tracked its path. I was entirely content. There was nothing I needed to accomplish. There was nothing wrong. I was just there, noticing, being alive. And I remember that feeling, even now. I remember how complete it was.

We tell children to stop daydreaming and pay attention, meaning pay attention to what we're trying to teach them. But maybe what we're really teaching them is how to not pay attention to most of what's actually happening. Maybe we're teaching them how to tune out. And we're never really taught how to tune back in, so most of us spend the rest of our lives in a state of mild distraction, our real lives happening in the background while we chase some version of success that might not actually be what we want.

I don't say any of this as a criticism, by the way. This is how the system is designed to work. And in many ways, it works fine. You need to be able to focus on your job to keep your job. You need to be able to manage your time to get things done. There's nothing wrong with productivity or achievement. But I think there's a real cost to organizing your entire life around these values and forgetting that the other kind of presence—the kind that my grandmother had, the kind that poets practice, the kind that I sometimes find in my car during lunch—is also necessary. It's necessary for your soul, I want to say, even if that sounds overly romantic. You need to notice your own life. You need to actually be alive, not just pushing through a series of tasks that accumulate into a life.

So I'm trying to practice this more consciously now. I try to look at people—really look at them—for a few seconds longer than is comfortable. I try to taste my food instead of just consuming it. I try to listen to conversations instead of thinking about what I'll say next. I try to notice the details of the places I go frequently, the way the light changes, the way the seasons turn. I try to be present for the small moments instead of always waiting for the significant ones. And it's strange because on the surface nothing is different. I'm not happier in any obvious way. I'm not more successful. But I'm more here. And that turns out to matter more than I would have expected.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, though that word has become so commercialized and turned into another thing to accomplish that I'm reluctant to use it. I'm talking about something simpler and older: just paying attention. Being here now. Noticing. And maybe that's what I really wanted to say—that there's a richness available in simple presence that we're mostly trained to overlook. That your one actual life is happening right now, and it's made up almost entirely of small moments that don't seem to matter, but they do. They matter because they're real. They matter because they're yours. They matter because you're noticing them.
